meta.tagline: Duolingo won't teach you this — Germany edition (plus Bayern mode).

categories.title: Ordering a beer/food like a local (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You're at a German bar and they ask what you'd like to drink.

question.en: What would you like to drink? (formal Sie)

answers.en: A pale lager, please — common in the south.

likelyReply.es: Vom Fass oder aus der Flasche?

exchanges.notes: "Ein Helles" is the southern default. Servers open with the formal Sie.

situation.en: You've ordered a beer and they ask how you want it.

question.es: Vom Fass oder aus der Flasche?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: In a Munich beer garden, they ask what size beer you want.

exchanges.notes: Size is its own question, asked after you've said what you want and whether it's draft. It's a Bavarian one: a Maß is the litre stein, a Halbe the half-litre. Order a Maß in Hamburg and you'll get a look. Die Maß is feminine, so it's eine Maß, not einen.

situation.en: They ask whether you want something to eat as well.

question.es: Möchten Sie auch was zu essen?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You're paying as a group and they ask how.

exchanges.notes: Splitting the bill is completely normal and expected.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You want to know which beers they have on draft before you choose.

question.en: What have you got on tap?

answers.en: Pils, pale lager and a wheat beer.

exchanges.notes: Asking this rather than pointing at a tap handle is most of the difference.

situation.en: Your glass is empty and the server catches your eye.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: It's late and the bartender offers you one last small drink.

answers.es: Nein, ich muss morgen früh raus.
answers.en: No, I've got an early start.

exchanges.notes: Ein Absacker is the last drink of the night — literally the one that makes you sink.

categories.title: Starting a convo/basic survival (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: Someone greets you.
Someone asks how you're doing.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You need help and want to check whether they speak English.

exchanges.notes: "Sprechen Sie Englisch?" is the formal version — use it with staff, officials and anyone much older. Same question, different register.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You didn't catch what someone just said.

exchanges.notes: "Ich check's nicht" is casual — fine with peers, not in a formal setting.

situation.en: You don't know a word and want to ask what it is.

question.en: How do you say [WORD] in German?

situation.en: You're looking for a place and stop someone to ask.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: A German friend greets you with a single syllable and then waits.

answers.en: Hey! — mirroring it back is the correct answer.

exchanges.notes: "Na?" is a complete greeting on its own. Answering "Na!" is not a dodge — it is the reply.

situation.en: You've been chatting a while and realise you never said your name.

note.es: Slang level: medium → heavy. Items marked young are more common with younger people, online, and in friend groups.
note.en: If you want local but safe, use the ones without a young badge. Items marked very casual are not for work.

phrases.en: Intense / crazy / wow.
Awesome. Can sound crude in other contexts, but common as "cool".
Super.
For sure.
Solid / good.
It's going / all good.
Awesome — literally "hammer".
Insane / unbelievable — good or bad, tone decides.
(Not) in the mood / up for it.
I'm in.
I can't be bothered with that.
Do you fancy it?
Definitely — clipped from "auf jeden Fall".
I'd rather not.
Doesn't work for me right now.
I'm out — count me out of this one.
Dude! / bro! — tone matters.
Bro / dude. Very casual.
Bro.
Guys! — the safe one for a whole group.
Man! — frustration or emphasis, never a word for a person.
Mate — jokey and slightly ironic between friends.
Love / hon — partners and close family only.
Lads / girls — calling over a mixed group.
No idea. Shortened to "kp" in texts.
I swear.
Are you clueless? Can come across as rude.
Exactly — and, just as often, pure filler while they think.
Ohh, I see — the realisation noise.
Seriously?
Nonsense! / rubbish!
Yes and no — ja plus nein, and a real dictionary word.

categories.title: Bayern slang / Bavarian flavour
categories.description: Identity language for Bavaria and parts of Austria

note.es: Standard German works everywhere. Bavarian is regional identity language — use it in Bayern and Austria.
note.en: Don't drop it in Hamburg and expect the same vibe. Outside the south you'll sound very regional.

phrases.en: Hi / bye (informal).
Hello.
Bye — singular / plural.
Hello, to one person — warmer and more local than Servus.
Hello, to a group.
Pleased to meet you — literally "I have the honour".
Goodbye — the southern version of auf Wiedersehen.
Hello everyone — greeting a whole table at once.
Emphasis particle — roughly "you know" / "mind you" / "really".
Sighing interjection: "oh man…".
Nonsense! — literally a shredded pancake.
Don't rush! — a whole philosophy in two words.
We'll see — the Bavarian shrug.
A little bit.
Daft, silly — mild enough to say to a friend.
A professional grump — said with real affection.
It's fine / all good.
I like you — dialect-y.
We are who we are — Bavaria's unofficial motto.
The bread-and-cold-cuts meal — a fixed part of the day, not a snack.
A bread roll — a Brötchen everywhere north of here.
A half-litre of beer — the everyday order, not the tourist litre.
Beer with lemonade — orderable anywhere in Bayern without comment.
Squirrel's tail — the pronunciation test a local will eventually set you.

note.es: Profanity is common, but don't use it with strangers unless you really know the vibe.

phrases.en: Shit.
Damn.
A milder "crap".
Man! / oh come on! — completely safe in any company.
Darn! — the polite one.
Damn it all — stronger than Verdammt, still not aimed at anyone.
Good heavens!
Well I never! — admiration or annoyance, tone decides which.
Shut it.
Piss off.
Leave me alone — firm, and not a swear word.
Stop bugging me.
That's enough now.
Oh sh*t! — a reaction to a situation, not aimed at a person.
Total idiot — keep it for telling the story, not for the person.
Get lost — everyday among friends, never with a stranger.

categories.title: Calling someone attractive (Germany)
categories.description: Flirt lines that don't land badly

note.es: Only flirt if it feels mutual. Keep it light and accept a no immediately.
note.en: Back off without arguing or guilt-tripping.

phrases.en: You look good.
You're really cute.
I like your style.
You have a nice smile.
You have beautiful eyes.
You've got a lovely laugh.

phrases.es: Mit dir kann man gut reden.
phrases.en: You're easy to talk to.
I really like you — warm, and not a come-on.
I find you attractive.

phrases.es: Hast du Lust auf ein Bier?
phrases.en: Want to grab a beer?
I like you.
Shall we go somewhere else?
Are you staying a bit longer?
I'd like to see you again.
Can I have your number?

phrases.es: Das war ein schöner Abend mit dir.
phrases.en: That was a lovely evening with you.
No pressure if not.
All good, I respect that.
Honestly, no problem.
I'll leave you to it.
It was good to meet you.
All good — enjoy your night.
Sorry, I misread that.
I didn't mean to be pushy.
Can I tell you something?

phrases.es: Ist es okay, wenn ich dich auf einen Drink einlade?
phrases.en: Is it okay if I ask you for a drink?
Is this okay with you?
Do you want me to go?

phrases.es: Sag einfach, wenn's zu viel ist.
phrases.en: Just say if it's too much.
May I sit down?
Would you rather be on your own?
Are you comfortable with this?

categories.title: Getting around (taxi + metro) (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've landed and you're looking for where the taxis are.

question.en: Where do I find a taxi?

answers.en: Outside, in front of the exit.

exchanges.notes: Works for the bus and the train too — swap Taxi for Bus or Zug.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: Before getting in, you want to know what a taxi into town costs.

question.en: What does it cost to the centre?

exchanges.notes: Ask before the bags go in the boot, not after.

situation.en: You've landed and want the train into the city rather than a taxi.

question.es: Wo ist der Zug in die Stadt?
question.en: Where's the train into the city?

situation.en: An officer at the border asks for your documents.

answers.en: One moment, I'll get it out.

situation.en: You need to collect your suitcase and can't see which way to go.
You want a transport ticket and can't find anywhere to buy one.

question.es: Wo kann ich ein Ticket kaufen?
question.en: Where can I buy a ticket?

situation.en: Customs stops you on the way out of the airport.
You have your bag and just need to get out of the terminal.
You get into a taxi and the driver asks where to.
You've arrived and want the driver to pull over.
You're at the taxi with a heavy suitcase and need the boot opened.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You've arrived and the driver asks how you're settling up.

question.es: Zahlen Sie bar oder mit Karte?
question.en: Are you paying cash or card?

exchanges.notes: Plenty of German taxis are still cash-first. Ask before you get in if you have no notes.

situation.en: You've spotted your street and want to get out before the corner.
You're running late and want to know how long the ride will take.

question.en: Roughly how long will it take?

situation.en: You need the fare receipted so you can expense the trip.
The driver reads the address back to you before setting off.
You're on the street looking for the U-Bahn.
You know your destination but not which line to take.

question.en: I need to go to [PLACE]. Which line?

situation.en: You're on the platform and want to know if the line goes straight there.
You're on board and want to know how far your stop is.
It's well past midnight and you don't know if the line is still running.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: An inspector in plain clothes asks to see your ticket mid-journey.

exchanges.notes: German metros have no barriers — inspectors board at random and a missing ticket is a 60-euro fine.

situation.en: Two platforms serve the same line and you don't know which one you want.
You're on a platform and want someone to confirm you're on the right side.

question.es: Ist das hier die richtige Seite?
question.en: Am I on the right side?

categories.title: At a restaurant (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You arrive at a restaurant with one other person.

question.es: Haben Sie einen Tisch für zwei?

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've finished eating and want to pay.

exchanges.notes: Cash is still common — plenty of places are card-shy.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You want tap water rather than bottled.

exchanges.notes: Tap water isn't automatic in Germany — you have to ask for it by name.

situation.en: You've been at the table a few minutes and the server comes over.

likelyReply.en: I'll come back in a moment.

situation.en: The menu means nothing to you and you'd rather be told what's good.

answers.en: The schnitzel is the most popular.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've decided and want to order your main course.

answers.en: Of course. Anything to drink with that?

exchanges.notes: "Ich hätte gern" is the polite default for ordering anything, food or drink.

situation.en: A plate arrives that isn't what you asked for.

question.es: Entschuldigung, das habe ich nicht bestellt.
question.en: Excuse me, I didn't order this.

answers.es: Oh, Entschuldigung — ich tausche es um.

situation.en: The server clears your plate and asks how the food was.

categories.title: Checking in (hotel/hostel/Airbnb) (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You arrive at the hotel desk and need to claim your booking.

question.es: Ich habe eine Reservierung auf den Namen [NAME].

answers.en: One moment, I'll look it up.

likelyReply.es: Kann ich bitte Ihren Pass sehen?

situation.en: You walk in without booking ahead and they ask at the desk.

answers.es: Nein, haben Sie noch ein Zimmer frei?
answers.en: No — do you have a room free?

situation.en: You want to know whether breakfast costs extra.

answers.es: Nein, das kostet zehn Euro extra.

situation.en: You're planning your last morning and need the checkout time.

question.en: When do I have to check out?

situation.en: Your train is this evening but the room is gone at eleven.

question.en: Can I leave my luggage here?

answers.es: Klar, wir stellen es in den Gepäckraum.
answers.en: Sure, we'll put it in the luggage room.

situation.en: You're in the room and want to get online.
They hand you the key and tell you where to go.

likelyReply.en: Round the corner on the right.

situation.en: You've dropped your bags and want dinner without walking far.

question.es: Gibt es hier in der Nähe was zu essen?
question.en: Is there anywhere to eat nearby?

answers.es: Zwei Straßen weiter gibt's einen Italiener.
answers.en: Two streets down there's an Italian place.

subsections.title: When something's wrong with the room

situation.en: The room is freezing and the radiator is doing nothing.

answers.en: I'll send someone up right away.

situation.en: Your room faces a busy street and you can't sleep.

answers.es: Ich kann Ihnen ein Zimmer zum Hof geben.
answers.en: I can give you a room facing the courtyard.

situation.en: There's no hot water in the shower.

answers.es: Das tut mir leid — ich melde es sofort.
answers.en: I'm sorry — I'll report it right away.

situation.en: You have an early flight and don't trust your alarm.

question.es: Können Sie mich um sieben wecken?
question.en: Could you wake me at seven?

situation.en: The door shut behind you and your key is on the bed.

question.es: Ich habe meinen Schlüssel im Zimmer gelassen.

answers.es: Kein Thema, ich komme mit hoch.
answers.en: Not a problem, I'll come up with you.

situation.en: There's one towel between two of you.
You've decided to stay on and want to extend the booking.

question.es: Können wir eine Nacht länger bleiben?
question.en: Can we stay one more night?

answers.es: Ich schaue, ob das Zimmer frei ist.
answers.en: I'll see whether the room is free.

situation.en: You're handing the key back and they ask about your stay.

categories.title: Shops, supermarkets & Pfand (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You've been browsing a minute and an assistant comes over.

likelyReply.en: Just say if you need anything.

situation.en: The only one on the rail is too small for you.

question.es: Haben Sie das eine Nummer größer?
question.en: Do you have this one size bigger?

situation.en: You want to try something on before buying it.

answers.en: Sure, the fitting rooms are at the back.

situation.en: There's no price tag on the thing you want.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You have no cash and want to check before queueing.

exchanges.notes: Worth asking first. Plenty of small German shops, bakeries and bars are still cash-only.

situation.en: What you bought yesterday doesn't fit and you want to swap it.
You're at the till with an armful and no bag.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: It's late afternoon and you want to know if you can come back tomorrow.

exchanges.notes: Sunday closing is near-total in Germany. Plan Saturday, or find a Späti or a station shop.

situation.en: You hand over a fifty for a four-euro shop.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've carried a bag of empty bottles in and can't see the machine.

answers.en: Back left, next to the entrance.

exchanges.notes: Pfand is 8–25 cents a bottle. The machine prints a voucher you hand in at the till.

situation.en: The queue moves and the cashier calls you forward.
You're deciding between two bottles and want to know which one you get money back on.

question.en: Is there a deposit on that?

situation.en: You've walked every aisle and still can't find the milk.
The cashier asks about a loyalty card before ringing you up.

question.en: Do you have a loyalty card?

situation.en: You've picked up loose apples and there's no price on them.

question.es: Muss ich das Obst selbst wiegen?
question.en: Do I have to weigh the fruit myself?

answers.es: Ja, an der Waage da drüben.
answers.en: Yes, at the scale over there.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Your shopping is piling up at the end of the belt faster than you can pack.

question.en: Do you want to start packing?

exchanges.notes: German checkouts move fast and you bag your own shopping while they scan. Nobody will help — it is not rudeness.

categories.title: Berlin slang / Berliner Schnauze
categories.description: The capital's own dialect — blunt, fast and warm underneath.

note.es: Die Berliner Schnauze klingt grob und ist es nicht.
note.en: Berliners sound brusque and mean nothing by it. The bluntness is the friendliness — take it at face value and answer in kind.

subsections.title: Berlinerisch — the words that give it away

phrases.en: I — Berlin's own version of ich.
What — wat and det replace was and das.
That.
Brilliant — old Berlin, still said with a wink.
Great — same vintage as knorke, same wink.
Not happening — "gibt es nicht" in a Berlin mouth.
Eh? / right? — the tag stuck on the end of everything.
Look at that! — "guck mal" up here.

subsections.title: Späti, Kiez and what things are called here

phrases.en: The late-night corner shop — a Berlin institution and your 2am friend.
Your neighbourhood — Berliners identify with theirs more than with the city.
A bread roll — a Brötchen elsewhere, a Semmel in Bayern.
A jam doughnut. A pancake here is an Eierkuchen — order carefully.
A meat patty — a Frikadelle in most of the country.
A sandwich — a buttered slice with something on top.
A beer for the walk — legal in public and completely unremarkable.
The corner pub — cheap, old, open late, and nothing like a bar.

categories.title: Nightlife — the door, the club, the people (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You reach the front of the queue and the bouncer counts your group.
The bouncer looks at you and wants to know your age.
You're at the front and want to know what you'll be paying.

question.en: How much is it to get in?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: The bouncer looks past you and turns you away without a reason.

answers.en: Fair enough, have a good night.

exchanges.notes: Berlin doors give no reason and you do not ask for one. Taking it well is the entire etiquette — arguing guarantees it again.

situation.en: It's early and you want to know whether to come back later.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You're through the door and someone reaches for your phone.

exchanges.notes: Standard in Berlin clubs. No photos inside, the tape stays until you leave, and people relax because of it.

situation.en: It's cold outside and you don't want to carry your coat all night.

answers.en: Cloakroom's on the right, three euros.

situation.en: You're stepping outside for air and they offer you a stamp.

likelyReply.en: See you in a bit, then.

situation.en: You're talking to people at the bar and want to keep it going.
This place is dying and you'd rather go on with the people you've met.
Someone at the bar notices you're standing by yourself.

question.en: Are you here on your own?

situation.en: The group you've joined is leaving and you want to tag along.

question.en: Where are you going after this?

answers.es: In den Club um die Ecke.
answers.en: To the club round the corner.

situation.en: You've been talking for ten minutes and lost their name immediately.
Someone you've been talking to offers to get the next round.
It's late and you want to leave without it being a whole thing.

likelyReply.en: It was good — see you soon!

situation.en: The bar you're in is dead and you want a local's recommendation.

question.en: Do you know anywhere good round here?

answers.es: Zwei Straßen weiter, der ist besser.
answers.en: Two streets over — that one's better.

phrases.en: To pre-drink — literally "to pre-glow".
Closing time — largely theoretical in Berlin.
The bouncer — the person who decides how your night goes.
To dance it properly out of your system.
To go big tonight.
To go straight through until morning.
In one — downing a drink in a single go.
The after-work beer — an institution rather than an event.

categories.title: How drunk are you? (Germany)
categories.description: The whole ladder, and the moments where you have to pick a rung out loud.

note.en: German grades drunkenness finely and nobody is coy about it. Naming your rung honestly is normal, and it is how people decide whether to put you in a taxi.

phrases.en: Tipsy, in the nicest way — from schwippen, to sway.
Merry — the polite one, safe at a work party.
To have had a few — literally "to have one sitting".
To be drunk — literally "to be blue".
Drunk — the standard, neutral word.
Plastered — informal, a bit crude, very common.
Hammered — Berlin's own, and said with some pride.
Falling-down drunk.
Someone who has gone under — literally a "schnapps corpse".
Completely gone.

situation.en: A few drinks in, a friend checks how you're doing.

answers.en: All good — only two beers in.

situation.en: Someone is working out whether to order you another round.
You stand up and realise the room is doing something it shouldn't.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone arrives at the table with a tray of shots for everyone.

answers.es: Nee, ich bin schon gut dabei.
answers.en: Nah, I'm well on my way already.

exchanges.notes: "Gut dabei sein" is the graceful refusal — it admits you're drunk without making it a problem.

situation.en: You've hit your limit and want to stop before it stops you.

answers.es: Dann hör auf, ist doch okay.

situation.en: A stranger has noticed the state your friend is in.

answers.es: Der ist ziemlich besoffen, ich bring ihn heim.
answers.en: He's pretty plastered — I'm taking him home.

likelyReply.en: Do you two need a taxi?

situation.en: It's the next day and you're owning up to how last night went.

question.en: I was completely gone last night.

situation.en: You're leaving and someone wants to know you'll make it home.

question.en: Can you manage on your own?

situation.en: The round is going in and you'd rather sit this one out.
It's your round and you want something soft without a discussion.

question.es: Nur ein Wasser für mich, bitte.
question.en: Just a water for me, please.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You drove here and want that understood before anyone offers.

exchanges.notes: Germany's limit is 0.5, and 0.0 for your first two years of licence. "Ich fahre" ends the conversation — nobody pushes.

situation.en: Someone won't take your first no about one more drink.
You've drunk more than you've eaten and you can feel it.
You've decided the night is over for you.
A friend is pacing you and pushes a glass of water over.
You're outside the bar and in no state to work out a night bus.

question.es: Kannst du mir ein Taxi rufen?
question.en: Could you call me a taxi?

categories.title: The morning after & the pharmacy (Germany)

situation.en: Your head is splitting and you need something for it.

question.en: Do you have anything for a headache?

question.en: What seems to be the matter?

situation.en: You feel wrecked and want to explain why.

phrases.en: The hangover — literally "the tomcat".
Hungover.
The hangover breakfast — salty, and a genuine institution.
Hair of the dog — literally the "counter-beer".
A blackout — literally the film tearing mid-reel.
What's still in you this morning — the word that stops you driving.
To be desperately thirsty the day after — literally to have a fire.
Never again. Said sincerely, roughly monthly.

categories.title: Robbed, lost & emergencies (Germany)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: You reach for your wallet on the U-Bahn and it isn't there.
You need to report it and don't know where to go.

situation.en: Someone in your group is hurt and needs seeing to.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: A stranger has stopped to help and is reaching for their phone.

exchanges.notes: 112 is the Europe-wide emergency number: free, works from any phone, and works without a SIM.

situation.en: Your phone died and you have no way to call anyone.
You're asking around the bar for a charger.
You need to reach someone and your phone is useless.

question.en: Could I make a quick call?

situation.en: You have no data and need to look up where you are.

answers.es: Ja, Passwort steht an der Wand.

situation.en: Roaming is costing you a fortune and you want a local SIM.

question.es: Kannst du mir eine SIM-Karte empfehlen?
question.en: Can you recommend a SIM card?

answers.en: At the phone shop in the station.

situation.en: You're standing on a corner looking visibly lost and someone stops.

likelyReply.en: Where are you trying to get to?

situation.en: The trains have stopped and you need any way home at all.

question.en: How do I get out of here?

answers.en: Night bus M10, just up there.

situation.en: The bar is cash-only and your pockets are empty.

answers.en: There's a cash machine in the Späti.

categories.title: For the girls (Germany)
categories.description: What it sounds like, and how to end it.

note.en: Every line here is meant to be said at normal volume or louder. Germans will not think you are overreacting — bar and club staff are trained for exactly this.

subsections.title: What it sounds like & shutting it down

situation.en: A man you don't know steps into your path outside a bar.

question.en: Hey gorgeous, all on your own?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone tells you to smile as you walk past.

question.en: Come on, give us a smile!

exchanges.notes: The comeback is the tell: a man who calls you a Zicke for declining was never being friendly.

situation.en: Someone has been talking at you for five minutes and won't take a hint.

question.en: I want to be left alone.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: A stranger puts a hand on your waist in a crowded bar.

exchanges.notes: Say it loudly. The volume is the point — it turns heads, and that is what makes it stop.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: A man insists on buying you a drink you didn't ask for.

answers.en: Thanks, I've already got a drink.

exchanges.notes: Never accept a drink you didn't watch being poured, however well it's meant.

situation.en: Polite has stopped working and you're done being polite.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You get the bartender's attention about the man who won't leave.

exchanges.notes: German bar staff will act on this. Say it to them rather than to your friends.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You want the fastest exit line, whether or not it's true.

question.es: Ich bin mit meinem Freund hier.

exchanges.notes: It shouldn't work better than no. It often does. Use whatever ends it fastest.

situation.en: You want someone with you between the door and the taxi.

question.es: Kannst du mich zum Taxi bringen?
question.en: Can you walk me to a taxi?

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: Nothing has happened yet but you want to leave anyway.

question.es: Ich fühl mich hier nicht wohl.

exchanges.notes: You never have to justify this one. "Nicht wohl" is reason enough for any German friend.

situation.en: You don't want to be on your own for the next few minutes.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: Two sips in, your drink has hit you far harder than it should have.

question.es: Ich glaube, mir wurde was ins Glas getan.
question.en: I think something was put in my drink.

exchanges.notes: Tell the bar staff, not only your friends. German clubs take this seriously and have a procedure for it.

situation.en: A bartender has clocked that something is wrong and offers to step in.
You're leaving alone and want someone to know you got back.

question.es: Ich schreib dir, wenn ich zu Hause bin.
question.en: I'll text you when I'm home.

situation.en: He's waiting outside and you'd rather not walk out yet.

question.es: Kann ich hier warten, bis er weg ist?
question.en: Can I wait here until he's gone?

answers.en: Of course — as long as you like.

situation.en: Your group is drifting towards the door and you don't want to be last.
